claims.text: The initial material is a thin-film FeNiCrCoCu coating on a conventional metal substrate.
The initial FeNiCrCoCu coating is nanocrystalline.
The initial FeNiCrCoCu coating is metastable.
The proposed intervention is to increase the test temperature from approximately 25°C to approximately 500°C under otherwise comparable loading conditions.
Elevated temperature increases atomic mobility at grain boundaries in the FeNiCrCoCu coating.
Increased grain-boundary mobility facilitates dynamic structural relaxation during sliding contact.
Dynamic structural relaxation redistributes stress and reduces localized stress concentrations.
Reduced local stress concentrations delay dislocation nucleation during nanoscale contact.
Grain-boundary relaxation lowers the effective friction coefficient under mechanical loading.
Grain-boundary relaxation reduces plastic deformation under mechanical loading.
Testing at approximately 500°C will produce a lower effective friction coefficient than testing at approximately 25°C.
Testing at approximately 500°C will produce less localized plastic deformation than testing at approximately 25°C.
High-temperature tests will show smoother residual indent profiles than room-temperature tests.
High-temperature tests will show a delayed yield point relative to room-temperature tests.
Lower friction and reduced localized plastic deformation indicate improved high-temperature sliding wear resistance.
The proposed mechanism applies approximately within 400–500°C under loading typical of nanoindentation.
The proposed temperature regime has minimal oxidation effects.
At more extreme temperatures, severe oxidation may dominate wear behavior.
Film–substrate adhesion and oxidation near the upper temperature boundary may alter the magnitude of the predicted wear improvement.
